content:
The FDA is telling consumers, restaurants and retailers not to eat, sell or serve raw oysters harvested by the Little Wicomico Oyster Company of Heathsville, Virginia, between Sept. 18 and Oct. 8, 2026 — and Texas is among the states that received them.

The advisory, posted Oct. 19, follows a multistate outbreak of Salmonella Telelkebir. The CDC counts 27 confirmed illnesses across 12 states, with five of the 21 patients with available information hospitalized. No deaths have been reported. Illnesses began between May 29 and Sept. 14, 2026.

The numbers, however, are disputed in a way shoppers should know about: Virginia's Department of Health counts 53 illnesses across 18 states tied to the same oysters, and says the CDC's 27 represent a genomic subgroup of the larger cluster. Either way, the guidance is identical — don't eat them.

How investigators connected the dots: of the sick people interviewed, 77% reported eating raw oysters — against a background rate of just 1.6% in the CDC's food survey. Traceback found Little Wicomico River oysters were the one harvest area all traced cases had in common, and a sample taken by Pennsylvania officials at a distributor tested positive for Salmonella (genome sequencing to confirm the outbreak strain is pending).

The oysters, carrying dealer code VA-1421-SP, were shipped to restaurants and retailers in 15 states and Washington, D.C.: California, Colorado, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Maryland, Missouri, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Texas, Virginia and D.C. Publix was the only major grocer to publicly confirm receiving them, selling them under the James River Oysters brand — and Georgia's agriculture department says Publix sold the recalled oysters through Oct. 14, five days after Virginia closed the Little Wicomico River to shellfish harvesting on Oct. 9. That lag is worth watching.

The company has recalled the affected harvest, stopped harvesting from the area and says it is cooperating with investigators. Anyone who still has these oysters should throw them out; restaurants and retailers should dispose of them or contact their distributor. Check the harvest tag for VA-1421-SP and dates between Sept. 18 and Oct. 8.

Sources: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (advisory, Oct. 19, 2026); CDC; Food Safety News (Oct. 20, 2026); Marler Blog.

— Walter Webb & Willa Webb, News Anchors, Webb Watch 956

title: Salmonella outbreak tied to raw oysters reaches Texas: throw out Little Wicomico harvest, FDA says
